question: How many companies outperformed the S&P 500?
steps: 'Outperformed' means a bigger price change than the index over the same days; no period is named, so this year.
The S&P 500 is named, even though only as the thing to beat, so the companies are its members: this is how broad the index's gain is.
Take the index's own change, from the fund that tracks it.
Count the members with a bigger change, out of the members that have one.
sql: WITH idx AS (SELECT change_period_pct AS index_change_pct FROM benchmarks WHERE key = 'S&P 500') SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE s.change_period_pct > idx.index_change_pct) AS beat, count(s.change_period_pct) AS members, any_value(idx.index_change_pct) AS index_change_pct FROM stocks s CROSS JOIN idx WHERE s.in_sp500
headline: {beat} of {members} S&P 500 members beat the index {period}, when the index changed {index_change_pct}.

question: how many stocks beat the s&p this year
steps: The S&P 500 is named, so the stocks are its members, measured against it.
This year: from the first close of the year.
Count the members whose change beats the S&P 500 fund's, out of those with a change.
sql: WITH idx AS (SELECT change_period_pct AS index_change_pct FROM benchmarks WHERE key = 'S&P 500') SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE s.change_period_pct > idx.index_change_pct) AS beat, count(s.change_period_pct) AS members, any_value(idx.index_change_pct) AS index_change_pct FROM stocks s CROSS JOIN idx WHERE s.in_sp500
headline: {beat} of {members} S&P 500 members beat the index {period}, when it changed {index_change_pct}.

question: How many stocks lagged the Dow in 2026?
steps: The Dow is named, so the stocks are its members, measured against it.
In 2026: from 2026-01-01; the year is not over, so up to the latest close.
Count the members whose change is below the Dow fund's, out of those with a change.
sql: WITH idx AS (SELECT change_period_pct AS index_change_pct FROM benchmarks WHERE key = 'Dow') SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE s.change_period_pct < idx.index_change_pct) AS lagged, count(s.change_period_pct) AS members, any_value(idx.index_change_pct) AS index_change_pct FROM stocks s CROSS JOIN idx WHERE s.in_dow
headline: {lagged} of {members} Dow members lagged the Dow {period}, when it changed {index_change_pct}.

question: How many US stocks beat the market this year?
steps: 'US stocks' with 'the market' means every listed stock, not one index's members; the market is the S&P 500 fund.
Across all stocks, leave out companies under $2bn, and say so.
Count those beating the S&P 500 fund this year, out of those with a change.
sql: WITH idx AS (SELECT change_period_pct AS index_change_pct FROM benchmarks WHERE key = 'S&P 500') SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE s.change_period_pct > idx.index_change_pct) AS beat, count(s.change_period_pct) AS companies, any_value(idx.index_change_pct) AS index_change_pct FROM stocks s CROSS JOIN idx WHERE s.market_cap_usd >= 2e9
headline: {beat} of {companies} US companies above $2bn beat the S&P 500 {period}, when it changed {index_change_pct}.

question: What share of Dow stocks are up this year?
steps: 'Up this year' means a price change above zero since the first close of the year.
Only the Dow's members count.
Divide the members that rose by the members with a change.
sql: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE change_period_pct > 0) AS up, count(change_period_pct) AS members, 100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE change_period_pct > 0) / count(change_period_pct) AS share_pct FROM stocks WHERE in_dow
headline: {up} of {members} Dow stocks are up {period}, a share of {share_pct}.

question: How many S&P 500 stocks have fallen more than 20% this year?
steps: Take the S&P 500 members' price change this year.
Count those below -20%, out of those with a change.
sql: SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE change_period_pct < -20) AS fell, count(change_period_pct) AS members FROM stocks WHERE in_sp500
headline: {fell} of {members} S&P 500 members are down more than 20% {period}.

question: Which tech stocks beat the S&P 500 this year and grew revenue more than 10%?
steps: Tech is the Technology sector; no index is named for the stocks, so every listed company above $2bn.
Keep those whose price change this year beats the S&P 500 fund's.
Keep those whose latest annual revenue grew more than 10%.
List them by price change.
sql: WITH idx AS (SELECT change_period_pct AS index_change_pct FROM benchmarks WHERE key = 'S&P 500') SELECT s.ticker, s.name, s.change_period_pct, s.change_period_pct - idx.index_change_pct AS vs_index_pp, s.revenue_growth_pct, s.market_cap_usd FROM stocks s CROSS JOIN idx WHERE s.sector = 'Technology' AND s.market_cap_usd >= 2e9 AND s.change_period_pct > idx.index_change_pct AND s.revenue_growth_pct > 10 ORDER BY s.change_period_pct DESC LIMIT 20
headline: {name} leads the technology companies above $2bn that beat the S&P 500 {period} with revenue growth above 10%: {change_period_pct}.

question: What is the median P/E of the S&P 500?

Take the median, and count how many it covers.
sql: SELECT median(pe_x) AS median_pe_x, count(pe_x) AS n, count(*) AS members FROM stocks WHERE in_sp500
headline: The median S&P 500 member trades at {median_pe_x} earnings, across the {n} of {members} members with a P/E.

question: How many S&P 500 companies have negative free cash flow?

headline: {negative} of {members} S&P 500 members had negative free cash flow in their latest annual report.

question: Which sector did best in the S&P 500 this year?
steps: Group the S&P 500 members by sector.
For each sector take the median price change this year and how many members it has.
Rank the sectors by that median.
sql: SELECT sector, median(change_period_pct) AS median_change_pct, count(change_period_pct) AS n FROM stocks WHERE in_sp500 AND sector IS NOT NULL GROUP BY sector ORDER BY median_change_pct DESC
headline: {sector} did best among S&P 500 sectors {period}: its median member changed {median_change_pct}.

question: Did the average S&P 500 stock beat the index this year?
steps: The average stock is the median member's price change this year.
The index is the S&P 500 fund's change.
The gap between them is in percentage points.
sql: WITH idx AS (SELECT change_period_pct AS index_change_pct FROM benchmarks WHERE key = 'S&P 500') SELECT median(s.change_period_pct) AS median_member_change_pct, any_value(idx.index_change_pct) AS index_change_pct, median(s.change_period_pct) - any_value(idx.index_change_pct) AS gap_pp FROM stocks s CROSS JOIN idx WHERE s.in_sp500
headline: The median S&P 500 member changed {median_member_change_pct} {period}, against {index_change_pct} for the index: a gap of {gap_pp}.

question: average operating margin of software companies

headline: The median software company with revenue above $100mn earns an operating margin of {median_operating_margin_pct} (mean {mean_operating_margin_pct}), across {n} companies.

question: which companies have more cash than debt and grew revenue over 20%
steps: Debt is borrowings as filed; companies with no borrowings tagged are left out rather than treated as debt-free.
Cash above borrowings, and revenue growth above 20% from a base above $50mn.

question: Who are the ten highest-paid CEOs?
steps: CEO pay is held for S&P 500 members, from each company's latest proxy statement.
Take each CEO's total pay as reported, in the company's latest fiscal year.
Rank from highest and keep the top ten.
sql: SELECT p.ticker, s.name, p.ceo, p.ceo_total_pay_usd, p.fiscal_year_end FROM pay p JOIN stocks s USING (ticker) WHERE p.ceo_total_pay_usd IS NOT NULL ORDER BY p.ceo_total_pay_usd DESC LIMIT 10
headline: {ceo} of {name} was the best-paid S&P 500 CEO in the company's latest fiscal year, at {ceo_total_pay_usd}.

question: Which CEOs were paid most while their shareholders did worst?

Set it beside the shareholder return over the same table: what $100 invested became.
List the best-paid CEOs among companies where $100 became less than $100.
sql: SELECT p.ticker, s.name, p.ceo, p.ceo_total_pay_usd, p.tsr_value_of_100, p.tsr_since FROM pay p JOIN stocks s USING (ticker) WHERE p.tsr_value_of_100 < 100 AND p.ceo_total_pay_usd IS NOT NULL ORDER BY p.ceo_total_pay_usd DESC LIMIT 10
headline: {ceo} of {name} was paid {ceo_total_pay_usd} while $100 in its shares since {tsr_since} became ${tsr_value_of_100}.

question: Which S&P 500 companies grew revenue fastest last quarter?
steps: Take each S&P 500 member's most recent quarter on file.
Compare its revenue with the same quarter a year earlier, from a base above $50mn.
Rank by that growth and keep the top ten.
sql: SELECT q.ticker, s.name, q.quarter_end, q.revenue_usd, q.revenue_growth_yoy_pct FROM quarters q JOIN stocks s USING (ticker) WHERE s.in_sp500 AND q.is_latest AND q.revenue_year_ago_usd >= 5e7 AND q.revenue_growth_yoy_pct IS NOT NULL ORDER BY q.revenue_growth_yoy_pct DESC LIMIT 10
headline: {name} grew revenue fastest among S&P 500 members in its latest quarter, to {quarter_end}: {revenue_growth_yoy_pct} on a year earlier, from a base above $50mn.

question: Which companies get the most revenue from China?
steps: China is a region: match it in each company's geographic segments and in its reporting segments, since some companies report by region (Apple's Greater China).
Keep one line per company, the larger where it reports China both ways.
Rank by revenue, and show what share of the company's total it is.
sql: SELECT g.ticker, s.name, g.kind, g.segment, g.revenue_usd, g.share_of_revenue_pct, g.fiscal_year_end FROM segments g JOIN stocks s USING (ticker) WHERE g.kind IN ('geography', 'business') AND g.segment ILIKE '%china%' QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY g.ticker ORDER BY g.revenue_usd DESC) = 1 ORDER BY g.revenue_usd DESC LIMIT 10
headline: {name} reports the most revenue from China: {revenue_usd} in the year to {fiscal_year_end}, {share_of_revenue_pct} of its total.

question: Where have insiders bought the most stock in the past three months?
steps: Take insiders' open-market purchases over the past three months.
Add up the dollars bought per company and count the insiders buying.
Rank by dollars bought and keep the top ten.
sql: SELECT i.ticker, s.name, sum(i.value_usd) AS bought_usd, count(DISTINCT i.insider) AS insiders, max(i.trade_date) AS last_trade FROM insider_trades i JOIN stocks s USING (ticker) WHERE i.side = 'buy' AND i.trade_date >= DATE 'TODAY' - INTERVAL 91 DAY GROUP BY i.ticker, s.name HAVING sum(i.value_usd) IS NOT NULL ORDER BY bought_usd DESC LIMIT 10
headline: Insiders at {name} bought the most in the past three months: {bought_usd}, by {insiders} insiders.

question: Which S&P 500 stocks did funds add to most last quarter?
steps: Take 13F holdings for S&P 500 members: all managers' shares in the latest quarter against the quarter before.

Rank by the change in shares held and keep the top ten.
sql: SELECT f.ticker, s.name, f.quarter_end, f.shares_change_pct, f.holders, f.new_holders FROM fund_holdings f JOIN stocks s USING (ticker) WHERE s.in_sp500 AND f.holders >= 20 AND f.shares_change_pct IS NOT NULL ORDER BY f.shares_change_pct DESC LIMIT 10
headline: Funds added most to {name} in the quarter to {quarter_end}: shares held changed {shares_change_pct}, with {new_holders} new holders.

question: In how many months this year did Microsoft beat the S&P 500?
steps: Microsoft is named, so the stock is Microsoft; the S&P 500 is only the thing to beat, through the fund that tracks it.
Take each month's last closing price, adjusted for splits, for both, starting from last December so January has a month to compare with.
Work out each month's change for both and compare them month by month.
Count the months Microsoft's change was bigger, out of the months this year.
sql: WITH m AS (SELECT ticker, date_trunc('month', date) AS month, arg_max(adj_close_usd, date) AS close FROM prices WHERE ticker IN ('MSFT', 'SPY') AND date >= DATE 'LAST_YEAR-12-01' GROUP BY ticker, month), r AS (SELECT ticker, month, 100 * (close / lag(close) OVER (PARTITION BY ticker ORDER BY month) - 1) AS change_pct FROM m) SELECT strftime(s.month, '%Y-%m') AS month, s.change_pct AS stock_change_pct, b.change_pct AS index_change_pct, s.change_pct > b.change_pct AS ahead, count(*) FILTER (WHERE s.change_pct > b.change_pct) OVER () AS beat, count(*) OVER () AS months FROM r s JOIN r b ON b.month = s.month AND b.ticker = 'SPY' WHERE s.ticker = 'MSFT' AND s.month >= DATE 'YEAR-01-01' ORDER BY s.month
headline: Microsoft beat the S&P 500 in {beat} of {months} months {period}, including this month to date.

question: What was Nvidia's worst day this year?
steps: Nvidia is ticker NVDA.
Take its daily closing prices, adjusted for splits, from the last days of last year so the first day of this year has one before it.
Work out each day's change on the day before, and list the biggest falls this year.
sql: WITH d AS (SELECT date, 100 * (adj_close_usd / lag(adj_close_usd) OVER (ORDER BY date) - 1) AS day_change_pct FROM prices WHERE ticker = 'NVDA' AND date >= DATE 'LAST_YEAR-12-01') SELECT date, day_change_pct FROM d WHERE date >= DATE 'YEAR-01-01' ORDER BY day_change_pct LIMIT 5
headline: Nvidia's worst day {period} was {date}, when it changed {day_change_pct}.

question: How far is Tesla below its high this year?
steps: Tesla is ticker TSLA.
Find its highest closing price this year, adjusted for splits, and the day it was set.
Compare the latest close with that high.
sql: SELECT arg_max(date, adj_close_usd) AS high_date, max(adj_close_usd) AS high_usd, arg_max(adj_close_usd, date) AS latest_usd, 100 * (arg_max(adj_close_usd, date) / max(adj_close_usd) - 1) AS from_high_pct FROM prices WHERE ticker = 'TSLA' AND date >= DATE 'YEAR-01-01'
headline: Tesla's latest close is {from_high_pct} from its high {period}, set on {high_date}.

question: Which S&P 500 stocks rose in the most months this year?
steps: The S&P 500 is named, so the stocks are its members.
Take each member's last closing price in each month, adjusted for splits, from last December.
Work out each month's change and count the months each stock rose.
Rank the members by months up, then by this year's change.
sql: WITH m AS (SELECT p.ticker, date_trunc('month', p.date) AS month, arg_max(p.adj_close_usd, p.date) AS close FROM prices p JOIN stocks s ON s.ticker = p.ticker AND s.in_sp500 WHERE p.date >= DATE 'LAST_YEAR-12-01' GROUP BY p.ticker, month), r AS (SELECT ticker, month, close / lag(close) OVER (PARTITION BY ticker ORDER BY month) - 1 AS ch FROM m) SELECT s.ticker, s.name, count(*) FILTER (WHERE r.ch > 0) AS months_up, count(r.ch) AS months, s.change_period_pct FROM r JOIN stocks s USING (ticker) WHERE r.month >= DATE 'YEAR-01-01' GROUP BY s.ticker, s.name, s.change_period_pct ORDER BY months_up DESC, s.change_period_pct DESC LIMIT 10
headline: {name} rose in {months_up} of {months} months {period}, the most of any S&P 500 member, and changed {change_period_pct}.

question: Which Dow stock had the biggest drawdown this year?
steps: The Dow is named, so the stocks are its members.
A drawdown is the fall from the highest close so far to a later close, so follow each member's daily closes, adjusted for splits, through the year.
Take each member's deepest fall from its high, and the day it hit bottom.
Rank the members by that fall, deepest first.
sql: WITH p AS (SELECT p.ticker, p.date, p.adj_close_usd / max(p.adj_close_usd) OVER (PARTITION BY p.ticker ORDER BY p.date ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) - 1 AS below_high FROM prices p JOIN stocks s ON s.ticker = p.ticker AND s.in_dow WHERE p.date >= DATE 'YEAR-01-01'), d AS (SELECT ticker, 100 * min(below_high) AS drawdown_pct, arg_min(date, below_high) AS low_date FROM p GROUP BY ticker) SELECT s.ticker, s.name, d.drawdown_pct, d.low_date, s.change_period_pct FROM d JOIN stocks s USING (ticker) ORDER BY d.drawdown_pct LIMIT 10
headline: {name} had the deepest fall from a high among Dow members {period}: {drawdown_pct}, at its low on {low_date}.

question: How did Tesla perform 3 days after earnings?
steps: Earnings days are the company's quarterly results announcements: events with kind 'results', is_earnings and its ticker.

Three days means three trading days after the results day: from the close on events.before_date (the last trading day before the results day, the price before the news whether it came before the open or after the close) to the close three trading days after the results day, with prices numbered in date order.
No period is named, so every results day on file: the price history begins in 2018, so the period is from 2018-01-01; give the median change, how many were up and the count, and list each one.
sql: WITH ev AS (SELECT date AS event_date, before_date FROM events WHERE ticker = 'TSLA' AND kind = 'results' AND is_earnings AND NOT scheduled AND date >= '2018-01-01'), px AS (SELECT date, adj_close_usd, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY date) AS rn FROM prices WHERE ticker = 'TSLA'), d0 AS (SELECT e.event_date, e.before_date, min(p.rn) AS rn0 FROM ev e JOIN px p ON p.date >= e.event_date GROUP BY e.event_date, e.before_date), w AS (SELECT d.event_date, pb.date AS from_date, p3.date AS to_date, 100 * (p3.adj_close_usd / pb.adj_close_usd - 1) AS change_pct FROM d0 d JOIN px pb ON pb.date = d.before_date JOIN px p3 ON p3.rn = d.rn0 + 3) SELECT event_date, from_date, to_date, change_pct, median(change_pct) OVER () AS median_change_pct, count(*) FILTER (WHERE change_pct > 0) OVER () AS up, count(*) OVER () AS n FROM w ORDER BY event_date DESC
headline: Tesla changed a median of {median_change_pct} over the three trading days after each of its {n} quarterly results {period}, rising after {up} of them.

question: How has the S&P 500 done on CPI release days?
steps: CPI release days are events with kind 'cpi' that have happened (not scheduled); the CPI comes out at 8:30 before the open, so the day's move is that day's close against the day before.
The S&P 500 is its fund's prices (SPY).
No period is named, so every release day on file, from 2018-01-01 where the price history begins: the median day change, how many days were up, the count, and each day's change.
sql: WITH px AS (SELECT date, adj_close_usd, lag(adj_close_usd) OVER (ORDER BY date) AS prev FROM prices WHERE ticker = 'SPY'), ev AS (SELECT date FROM events WHERE kind = 'cpi' AND NOT scheduled AND date >= '2018-01-01'), w AS (SELECT e.date, 100 * (p.adj_close_usd / p.prev - 1) AS day_change_pct FROM ev e JOIN px p ON p.date = e.date WHERE p.prev IS NOT NULL) SELECT date, day_change_pct, median(day_change_pct) OVER () AS median_day_change_pct, count(*) FILTER (WHERE day_change_pct > 0) OVER () AS up, count(*) OVER () AS n FROM w ORDER BY date DESC
headline: The S&P 500 changed a median of {median_day_change_pct} on the {n} CPI release days {period}, rising on {up} of them.

question: Alphabet capex as a share of revenue
steps: Take Alphabet's latest annual report.
Divide its capital expenditure by its revenue.
sql: SELECT ticker, name, capex_usd, revenue_usd, 100.0 * capex_usd / revenue_usd AS capex_share_pct, fiscal_year_end FROM stocks WHERE ticker = 'GOOGL'
headline: {name} spent {capex_share_pct} of its revenue on capital expenditure, {capex_usd} of {revenue_usd} in the year to {fiscal_year_end}.

question: Microsoft capex vs operating cash flow over the last 5 years
steps: Take Microsoft's last five fiscal years.
Set capital expenditure against the cash its operations brought in each year.
sql: SELECT fiscal_year, capex_usd, cf_operating_usd, 100.0 * capex_usd / cf_operating_usd AS capex_share_of_cash_pct FROM annual WHERE ticker = 'MSFT' AND capex_usd IS NOT NULL AND cf_operating_usd IS NOT NULL ORDER BY fiscal_year DESC LIMIT 5
headline: In fiscal {fiscal_year} Microsoft's capital expenditure was {capex_usd} against operating cash flow of {cf_operating_usd}, {capex_share_of_cash_pct} of it.

question: Which big chipmakers spend the most on research as a share of revenue?
steps: Take chipmakers worth over $10bn.
Divide each one's research spending by its revenue.
Rank them.
sql: SELECT ticker, name, rd_usd, revenue_usd, 100.0 * rd_usd / revenue_usd AS rd_share_pct FROM stocks WHERE industry ILIKE '%SEMICONDUCTOR%' AND market_cap_usd >= 1e10 AND rd_usd IS NOT NULL AND revenue_usd > 1e8 ORDER BY rd_share_pct DESC LIMIT 10
headline: {name} spends the most on research among chipmakers worth over $10bn, {rd_share_pct} of revenue.
